one_liner: AVX-512/AVX2 SIMD quicksort/select library beating std::sort on primitive arrays and key-derived struct sorts (object_qsort).
what_it_does: Provides SIMD-accelerated quicksort, quickselect, partial-sort, argsort/argselect, and key-value sort for built-in 16/32/64-bit integer and float types, plus object_qsort for sorting arbitrary C++ structs by a scalar key extracted via a lambda. The built-in-type routines are free functions with behavior equivalent to std::sort/std::nth_element/std::partial_sort/np.argsort, but a different call shape: pointer+size arguments instead of iterators, plus explicit hasnan/descending/nans_last flags. object_qsort takes an object array and a key-extraction lambda in place of a comparator and sorts the array in place. It ships as both header-only source and a buildable library, and is vendored as a submodule inside NumPy (np.sort/argsort/partition) and PyTorch (torch.sort).
how_it_is_fast: Built-in-type routines vectorize quicksort partitioning using AVX-512 compressstore instructions (with an AVX2 fallback), based on two cited SIMD-partitioning papers, and drop to bitonic sorting networks on AVX-512/AVX registers for arrays below a size threshold (64-512 elements). object_qsort does not vectorize struct comparisons directly: it extracts each object's key into a separate array, sorts the resulting (key, index) pairs with the SIMD keyvalue_qsort, then permutes the original object array into place with a scalar cycle-following swap loop. Its speedup therefore comes from the primitive keyvalue sort plus, for expensive keys like Euclidean distance, auto-vectorized key computation, not from vectorizing the object comparisons themselves.
when_to_use: Sorting arrays of built-in 16/32/64-bit ints, floats, or doubles (or key-value pairs) on x86-64 hardware with AVX2 or AVX-512, where std::sort's per-element comparator overhead dominates
Sorting an array of structs by one scalar key -- a single member or a computed metric like Euclidean/Manhattan/Chebyshev distance -- via object_qsort's key-extraction lambda
Need argsort/argselect/partial_qsort with built-in NaN placement control (nans_last) instead of hand-rolling NaN partitioning around std::sort/std::nth_element
Batch or offline sorts where allocating O(N) extra memory for keys and an index array is acceptable
Comfortable depending on code already proven at NumPy/PyTorch/OpenJDK vendoring scale rather than a smaller, newer project
when_not_to_use: Target hardware lacks AVX2/AVX-512, or is not x86-64 (no aarch64/ARM support)
Sort key isn't reducible to one scalar of 32 or 64 bits -- object_qsort's key_func must return exactly float/double/(u)int32/64, not a multi-field comparator
Memory-constrained settings: object_qsort needs O(N) extra space (a key array plus a uint32/64 index array) on top of the object array itself
Need numbers independently verified on disclosed hardware/compiler: the object_qsort chart names only 'a processor with AVX-512', no CPU model, compiler, or flags, and the numbers are first-party

Care about scaling on adversarial input distributions: an independent 2023 analysis (Voultapher sort-research-rs) found worse-than-O(N log N) scaling for the primitive AVX-512 qsort on a random_p5 pattern

integration.form: header-only (src/x86simdsort-static-incl.h, compile-time AVX2/AVX-512 selection) or static/shared lib (Meson build under lib/, runtime CPUID dispatch)
integration.dependencies: none for the core routines; googletest and Google Benchmark (>=1.9.2) only if building the optional test/benchmark suite; OpenMP optional for parallelizing qsort/argsort/keyvalue_qsort
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; GCC 8+ (GCC 12+ required for _Float16/AVX-512FP16), Clang 8.0+, MSVC 2019 16.8+, or Intel icx
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 or AVX-512 (exact subset varies: skylake-avx512 for 32/64-bit, icelake-client for 16-bit, sapphirerapids for _Float16); no aarch64/ARM
integration.thread_safety: not documented for concurrent calls on separate arrays; optional OpenMP-based internal parallelism for qsort/argsort/keyvalue_qsort on large arrays, off by default, capped at 16 threads via OMP_NUM_THREADS
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: built-in-type routines are behaviorally equivalent to std::sort/nth_element/partial_sort/argsort but use a different (non-iterator) call signature; object_qsort, the API this record's benchmark actually measures, takes a key-extraction lambda instead of a comparator and is not a drop-in replacement for std::sort(begin, end, comparator)

gotchas: object_qsort's gain shrinks as sizeof(T) grows or the key gets cheap to compute relative to swap cost, since the final struct permutation is a scalar cycle-following swap loop, not SIMD
object_qsort's key_func return type must be exactly 32 or 64 bits (float/double/int32/int64/uint32/uint64) or the call fails a static_assert at compile time
For built-in-type routines, hasnan defaults to false; if the array actually contains NaNs and hasnan isn't set true, behavior is undefined

GCC 16.0.1 with LTO enabled reportedly failed to build (issue #224, closed without a posted fix) when vendored into NumPy, due to an 'inlining failed: target specific option mismatch' error on an always_inline comparator
pick_this_over_siblings_when: A maintainer directly asked how this compares to vxsort-cpp (issue #12) and no comparison was ever produced, so there's no first-party head-to-head with that sibling. Pick x86-simd-sort over the other primitive-array sorters in this catalog (BlockQuicksort, Boost.Sort spreadsort, IPS4o, LearnedSort, fluxsort, quadsort, radix_sort) specifically when the workload is 'sort a struct by one field or a derived distance metric' via object_qsort, not a flat array of ints -- none of the other siblings' benchmarks target that struct/key-sort shape.
verified_claims_summary: Numbers come from x86-simd-sort's own README benchmark (benchmarks/bench-objsort.hpp, Google Benchmark, run with --benchmark_filter=*obj*), comparing object_qsort against std::sort on arrays of 3D Point structs (float or double x/y/z) sorted by one coordinate or by Manhattan, Euclidean, or Chebyshev distance from the origin, on an unspecified x86 processor with AVX-512 and no disclosed compiler or flags: up to ~5x faster for float (32-bit) keys and ~4x for double (64-bit) keys sorting by one coordinate, up to ~10x faster sorting by Euclidean distance.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-06-25); BSD-3-Clause. 'Copyable' fits since the src/ headers can be vendored standalone at compile time -- as NumPy, PyTorch, and OpenJDK already do -- while the runtime-dispatching library form requires a Meson build.
